config.title: Position: fixed and sticky

intro.title: Position: fixed and sticky
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple webpage with a navigation bar that stays fixed at the top of the screen and a section that sticks to the top as you scroll. You will learn how to use the CSS `position` property with the values `fixed` and `sticky` to control element placement relative to the viewport. The main technologies involved are CSS selectors and the `position`, `top`, and `z-index` properties. This beginner-friendly lesson will help you create interactive, scroll-aware layouts commonly seen in modern websites.
intro.usecase: Fixed and sticky positioning are essential for creating persistent UI elements that remain visible during user interaction. You'll use position: fixed for navigation bars that stay at the top of the screen while scrolling, cookie consent banners that remain at the bottom, and chat widgets that stay in the corner. Position: sticky is perfect for table headers that remain visible as you scroll through data tables, section headings in long documentation pages, and filter panels in e-commerce product listings. These techniques are fundamental for improving usability in dashboards, forms, and any application requiring persistent access to key controls.

objectives: Apply the `position: fixed` property to create a navigation bar that remains visible while scrolling
Configure a sticky header that transitions from relative to fixed positioning at a specific scroll point
Manipulate the `top`, `bottom`, `left`, and `right` properties to control the placement of fixed elements
Construct a sidebar with sticky positioning that remains within its parent container boundaries
Implement a fixed footer that stays anchored to the viewport bottom regardless of content length
Integrate z-index values with fixed and sticky elements to manage stacking context and visibility
Update element positioning dynamically by toggling between fixed and sticky behaviors based on viewport conditions

steps.title: Create a CSS file and set up the basic HTML structure
steps.instruction: Create a CSS file and add a container element with multiple sections inside it to serve as the foundation for positioning examples.
steps.hint: Start by creating a container div with several child divs or sections that will later be positioned.
steps.seedCode: /* Create a container with multiple sections */
steps.expectedOutcome: A CSS file is created with a container and multiple sections defined as the foundation for positioning examples.
successCriteria: The CSS file contains a .container selector and multiple .section selectors (or similar) as the basic structure.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have both a container element and multiple section elements defined in your CSS.
steps.feedbackWrong: The structure isn't quite right. You need to create a container with multiple sections inside it as the foundation for our positioning examples.

steps.title: Style the container and sections with basic layout
steps.instruction: Add CSS rules to style the container with width, margin, and padding, and style each section with height and background colors.
steps.hint: Set the container width to 100%, add margin and padding for spacing, then give each section a distinct height and background color.
steps.seedCode:
/* Create a container with multiple sections */

/* Add your container and section styling here */
steps.expectedOutcome: The container will have full width with spacing, and sections will be visible with different heights and colors.
successCriteria: Container has width, margin, and padding properties defined. Sections have height and background-color properties defined.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some styling, but make sure both container and sections have all the required properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The styling is missing or incorrect. Please add CSS for container width/margin/padding and section height/background colors.

steps.title: Introduce the position property and its values
steps.instruction: Add CSS comments explaining the five main values of the position property: static, relative, absolute, fixed, and sticky. Write a brief definition for each value.
steps.hint: Use CSS comment syntax /* ... */ to add explanatory text. Keep each definition concise - one line per value is sufficient.
steps.analogousExample:
/* CSS comment example: brief explanation */
/* position: static; - default flow of the document */
steps.expectedOutcome: The CSS file will contain clear comments explaining each position value with brief definitions.
successCriteria: CSS comments exist explaining all five position values (static, relative, absolute, fixed, sticky) with brief definitions
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some position value explanations, but make sure to include all five: static, relative, absolute, fixed, and sticky. Each should have a brief definition.
steps.feedbackWrong: The position property explanations are missing or incomplete. Add CSS comments that define all five position values: static, relative, absolute, fixed, and sticky.

steps.title: Create a fixed header element
steps.instruction: Add a CSS rule for a header element with class 'fixed-header' that uses position: fixed, stays at the top of the viewport, spans the full width, and has a background color.
steps.hint: Use the selector .fixed-header and set position: fixed, top: 0, left: 0, width: 100%, and a background property like background-color: #333.
steps.expectedOutcome: A CSS rule for .fixed-header is added with position: fixed, top: 0, left: 0, width: 100%, and a background property.
successCriteria: The .fixed-header selector exists with position: fixed, top: 0, left: 0, width: 100%, and a background property (e.g., background-color).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your .fixed-header rule includes all required properties: position: fixed, top: 0, left: 0, width: 100%, and a background property.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fixed header rule is missing or incomplete. Check that you've defined .fixed-header with position: fixed and the necessary positioning and styling properties.

steps.title: Style the fixed header with visual properties
steps.instruction: Add background color, padding, text color, and box-shadow to the fixed header styling.
steps.hint: You can use properties like background-color, padding, color, and box-shadow to style the header. For example: background-color: #333; padding: 1rem; color: white; box-shadow: 0 2px 5px rgba(0,0,0,0.2);
steps.expectedOutcome: The fixed header will have a dark background, white text, padding, and a subtle shadow, making it visually distinct.
successCriteria: The fixed header styling includes background-color, padding, color, and box-shadow properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some styling, but make sure to include all required properties: background-color, padding, color, and box-shadow.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fixed header styling is missing or incomplete. Add the required visual properties to enhance the header.

steps.title: Add content to demonstrate fixed positioning behavior
steps.instruction: Add enough text content inside each section to make the page scrollable, so you can see how the fixed header stays in place while scrolling.
steps.hint: Add several paragraphs or a long block of text inside each section element. You can use lorem ipsum text or any placeholder content.
steps.expectedOutcome: The page becomes scrollable with substantial content in each section, allowing you to observe the fixed header remaining at the top while scrolling.
successCriteria: Each section contains enough text content to extend beyond the viewport height, creating a scrollable page where the fixed header behavior is visible.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some content, but the page might not be scrollable yet. Try adding more paragraphs or longer text to each section so the content extends beyond the viewport height.
steps.feedbackWrong: The page doesn't appear to have enough content to be scrollable. Make sure you've added substantial text content inside each section element.

steps.title: Create a sidebar with fixed positioning
steps.instruction: Add a CSS rule for a sidebar element with position: fixed, positioned at the right side of the viewport, and give it basic styling like width, background color, and padding.
steps.hint: Use the selector .sidebar and set position: fixed, right: 0, and top: 0 to pin it to the top-right corner.
steps.expectedOutcome: A sidebar element is styled with fixed positioning and appears pinned to the right side of the viewport.
successCriteria: The CSS includes a .sidebar rule with position: fixed, right: 0, top: 0, and at least width, background-color, and padding properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your sidebar has position: fixed and is positioned with right and top properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The sidebar isn't fixed yet. Check that you've used position: fixed and set right and top values.

steps.title: Introduce position: sticky concept
steps.instruction: Add a CSS comment explaining how sticky positioning works with threshold properties like top, bottom, left, and right.
steps.hint: Write a comment that describes how sticky elements behave when scrolling and how the threshold properties define when they become fixed.
steps.analogousExample: /* sticky: element toggles between relative and fixed based on scroll position; uses top, bottom, left, or right to define the threshold */
steps.expectedOutcome: A comment is added that explains the behavior of position: sticky and mentions the threshold properties.
successCriteria: The comment includes an explanation of sticky positioning and references top, bottom, left, and right as threshold properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a comment about sticky positioning, but make sure to mention how it uses threshold properties like top, bottom, left, or right.
steps.feedbackWrong: The comment doesn't explain sticky positioning with threshold properties. Try describing how sticky elements toggle between relative and fixed based on scroll.

steps.title: Create a sticky navigation bar
steps.instruction: Add a navigation element inside a section and apply position: sticky with top value
steps.hint: Create a .sticky-nav class with position: sticky and top: 0. Place it inside one of your existing sections.
steps.expectedOutcome: A sticky navigation bar that sticks to the top of its parent section when scrolling
successCriteria: CSS includes a .sticky-nav class with position: sticky and top: 0
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your .sticky-nav class includes both position: sticky and a top value (like top: 0).
steps.feedbackWrong: The sticky navigation bar wasn't created correctly. You need to define a .sticky-nav class with position: sticky and a top value.

steps.title: Style the sticky navigation bar
steps.instruction: Add background color, padding, border, and text styling to the sticky navigation bar to make it visually distinct.
steps.hint: Use CSS properties like background-color, padding, border, and color to style the sticky navigation bar.
steps.expectedOutcome: The sticky navigation bar will have a background color, padding, border, and text styling applied.
successCriteria: The sticky navigation bar has background-color, padding, border, and color properties defined.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some styling, but make sure to include background-color, padding, border, and text color.
steps.feedbackWrong: The sticky navigation bar styling is missing or incomplete. Try adding background-color, padding, border, and color properties.

steps.title: Add multiple sticky elements to compare behavior
steps.instruction: Add a second sticky element inside a different section with a different top value (e.g., top: 50px).
steps.hint: Create a new CSS rule for a sticky element in another section, using position: sticky and a different top value than the navigation bar.
steps.expectedOutcome: The page will have two sticky elements that stick at different positions when scrolling, demonstrating how top values affect sticky behavior.
successCriteria: A second sticky element is defined with position: sticky and a different top value than the navigation bar.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your new element has position: sticky and a different top value (like top: 50px).
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've added a new sticky element with position: sticky and a different top value. Review the CSS rule structure.

steps.title: Compare fixed vs sticky positioning
steps.instruction: Add a CSS comment at the end of your file summarizing the key differences between fixed and sticky positioning.
steps.hint: Write a comment that explains how fixed positioning is relative to the viewport while sticky positioning is relative to its container with a threshold.
steps.analogousExample: /* Fixed: relative to viewport, stays in place during scroll. Sticky: relative to container, sticks after threshold. */
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a clear summary comment explaining the differences between fixed and sticky positioning at the end of your CSS file.
successCriteria: A CSS comment is added that mentions both fixed (viewport-relative) and sticky (container-relative with threshold) positioning.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a comment, but make sure it mentions both fixed (viewport-relative) and sticky (container-relative with threshold) positioning.
steps.feedbackWrong: Please add a CSS comment that explains the differences between fixed and sticky positioning.
